notes: HIV transmission appeal; Court of Appeal confirms informed consent requirement following Dica and dismisses conviction and sentence appeals.

enrichment.short_title: Konzani: informed consent to HIV transmission risk under section 20 OAPA 1861
key_facts: Feston Konzani, knowing he was HIV positive, had unprotected sexual intercourse with three women without disclosing his condition and infected each of them.
He was convicted at Teesside Crown Court of three counts of inflicting grievous bodily harm contrary to section 20 of the 1861 Act and sentenced to consecutive terms totalling 17 years.
Recklessness and transmission were formally admitted; the jury found none of the complainants willingly or consciously consented to the risk of contracting HIV.
The appellant did not give evidence and there was no basis to infer an honest belief in informed consent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction and sentence to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) following conviction on section 20 counts.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentences upheld as neither manifestly excessive nor wrong in principle.
enrichment.ratio: Following R v Dica, a defendant who conceals HIV status and recklessly transmits the virus may be guilty of section 20 GBH; consent is a defence only if it is informed and willing consent to the specific risk of HIV infection, and an honest belief in such consent requires some evidential foundation.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge should have left honest belief in consent to the jury
Whether consent to unprotected sex implied consent to the risk of HIV infection
Application of R v Dica and R v Barnes to multiple complainants
Appropriateness of consecutive sentences
linked_authorities: R v Dica [2004] EWCA Crim 1103
R v Barnes [2004] EWCA Crim 3246
R v Brown [1994] 1 AC 212

confidence.notes: Consent directions, Dica analysis and dismissal are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Attorney General's reference on one-punch manslaughter; two-year sentence increased to three-and-a-half years.

enrichment.short_title: Attorney General's Reference (Uddin): unduly lenient one-punch manslaughter sentence
key_facts: Ali Uddin, aged 24, punched 66-year-old Donald Hill once in the face on a residential street in Walsall, causing a fatal skull fracture.
The deceased had consumed six or seven pints of beer; two 11-year-old girls witnessed the incident; Uddin fled to Bangladesh before returning to face arrest.
Uddin was convicted of manslaughter after trial, having falsely claimed self-defence and that a co-defendant kicked the deceased.
Judge Chapman sentenced him to two years' imprisonment on 20 December 2004.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 against an unduly lenient manslaughter sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; sentence increased from two years to three-and-a-half years' imprisonment after double jeopardy adjustment.
enrichment.ratio: One-punch manslaughter cases vary greatly in seriousness; gratuitous violence in a residential street against an innocent elderly victim, witnessed by children, with false blame cast on the deceased and no guilty plea, may warrant a substantially higher sentence than two years.
legal_issues: Whether the two-year sentence for one-punch manslaughter was unduly lenient
Application of sentencing authorities including Kime and Welsh
Weight of public concern about street violence and child witnesses
Effect of false self-defence and flight on mitigation
linked_authorities: R v Kime [2004] EWCA Crim 3357
Attorney General's Reference No 100 of 2001 (R v Welsh)
R v Majali [2000] 2 Cr App R (S) 384

confidence.notes: Facts, aggravating features and increased sentence are clearly stated though many comparator cases were reviewed.

notes: Litigant-in-person section 288 challenge to peat extraction refusal; Forbes J dismissed all grounds and refused permission to appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Sweet v SoS: section 288 challenge to peat extraction refusal on Westhay Moor

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) (England and Wales) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Mr and Mrs Sweet sought planning permission for peat extraction and waterfowl habitat creation on 1.69 hectares at Westhay Moor within an SSSI, SPA and Ramsar site.
Somerset County Council refused permission; the Secretary of State dismissed their section 78 appeal on an inspector's recommendation.
The inspector held the environmental statement inadequate and the development inconsistent with the development plan and emerging minerals local plan.
Mr Sweet pursued a section 288 application in person, seeking substantive approval to harvest peat rather than limited quashing relief.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 challenging the Secretary of State's dismissal of a recovered planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; claimants ordered to pay defendants' costs; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 288 relief is confined to quashing unlawful decision-making; an inadequate environmental statement and conflict with development plan policies are lawful bases to dismiss a peat extraction appeal, and peat extracted for sale is a mineral within section 336(1) of the 1990 Act.
legal_issues: Whether peat extraction for sale constitutes mineral working requiring EIA
Adequacy of the environmental statement including revised statement
Scope of section 288 relief versus merits of planning refusal
Whether inspector's reasoning was irrational or Wednesbury unreasonable

confidence.notes: Inspector's conclusions on EIA inadequacy and mineral definition are fully analysed though many procedural exchanges concern costs.

notes: Liability trial on ferry man-overboard drowning; Forbes J found Stena and master negligent in rescue manoeuvre.

enrichment.short_title: Davis v Stena Line: negligence causing passenger drowning after man overboard
key_facts: Michael Davis went overboard from Stena's ferry Koningin Beatrix on 29 October 2000 on the Rosslare-Fishguard route.
He was spotted in the water and could have been rescued by a nearby vessel or helicopter had rescue been properly managed.
Captain Williams attempted to retrieve Mr Davis to the ferry; wave conditions and the bow encounter caused Mr Davis to drown before recovery.
Mrs Davis brought fatal accident and Law Reform Act claims against Stena for dependants and the estate; only liability was tried.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court liability trial in a fatal accident and Law Reform Act claim arising from a passenger man-overboard incident at sea.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for the claimant on liability; Mr Davis' death held caused by Stena's and the master's negligence and not by his own fault.
enrichment.ratio: A ferry operator and master owe passengers a duty to conduct man-overboard recovery with reasonable care; attempting retrieval in a manner that materially worsens sea conditions and causes drowning can constitute fault or neglect under the Athens Convention regime.
legal_issues: Whether Stena and Captain Williams were negligent in the man-overboard rescue
Application of the Athens Convention as scheduled to the Merchant Shipping Act 1995
Causation of drowning versus survivability if rescue had been properly executed
Whether contributory negligence by Mr Davis caused his death

confidence.notes: Detailed fact findings on rescue manoeuvres and explicit liability conclusion; quantum not tried.

notes: Whole-life order appeal after second homicide; Court of Appeal substituted 21 years 172 days minimum term applying Sullivan and Schedule 21.

enrichment.short_title: R v L: section 269(4) whole-life order quashed for sadistic murder of prostitute
key_facts: G.L., who had previously killed his wife with diminished responsibility accepted in 1987, murdered a 19-year-old prostitute in August 2003 after prolonged torture with a bayonet.
He failed to take prescribed medication, gave himself up in Scotland, and wrote that he had killed again and should have taken his medication.
The jury rejected diminished responsibility; the recorder imposed life imprisonment with section 269(4) early release provisions disapplied.
Psychiatric evidence was divided on whether mental disorder lowered culpability below the Homicide Act threshold.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a whole-life minimum term order under section 269(4) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 following murder conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; whole-life order quashed and replaced with a minimum term of 21 years and 172 days after remand credit.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 269 the judge setting a minimum term must assess seriousness only, not public protection which the life sentence and Parole Board provide; basing a section 269(4) order on dangerousness is an error, and Schedule 21 with transitional Schedule 22 adjustments governs the minimum term.
legal_issues: Whether the recorder erred by disapplying early release based on future dangerousness
Application of R v Sullivan, Schedule 21 starting points and paragraph 11C mental disorder mitigation
Transitional reduction under paragraph 10 of Schedule 22
Crediting 193 days on remand in custody
linked_authorities: R v Sullivan and others [2004] EWCA Crim 1762

confidence.notes: Detailed Sullivan/Schedule 21 analysis and substituted minimum term are explicit.

notes: Beazer Homes appeal on admissibility of abortive collaboration negotiations for construing section 106 agreement; appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Beazer Homes v Stroude: inadmissibility of separate negotiation evidence in section 106 construction
key_facts: Peter Stroude and Beazer Homes disputed implied access rights over Cartwright land to construct the Longstanton Bypass under a section 106 agreement dated 16 October 2000.
Stroude and Beazer had separately negotiated an abortive collaboration agreement that was never concluded.
Beazer sought to rely on those negotiations in opposing Stroude's summary judgment application for a right of entry.
Rimer J ruled the collaboration negotiation evidence inadmissible for construing the section 106 agreement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from an interlocutory ruling under CPR Part 32.1 excluding evidence of negotiations for a separate collaboration agreement in a section 106 construction dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; evidence of abortive collaboration negotiations held inadmissible on the construction of the section 106 agreement.
enrichment.ratio: Evidence of negotiations and subjective intentions for a separate uncompleted agreement is inadmissible to construe a formal section 106 agreement; the Prenn and Investors Compensation Scheme exclusion applies equally where the only utility of the evidence is to show what the parties did not intend the concluded contract to cover.
legal_issues: Whether negotiations for contract B are admissible to construe contract A
Application of Prenn v Simmonds and Investors Compensation Scheme
Whether preliminary admissibility hearings under CPR 32.1 are appropriate
Implication of a right of access over third-party land in a planning agreement
linked_authorities: Prenn v Simmonds [1971] 1 WLR 1381
Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896
Reardon Smith Line Ltd v Yngvar Hansen-Tangen [1976] 1 WLR 989

confidence.notes: Mummery and Munby LJJ give detailed Prenn-based reasoning and clear dismissal.

notes: Interim harassment injunction ruling in Save Newchurch Guinea Pigs campaign; exclusion zone refused pending trial of modified order.

enrichment.short_title: Hall v Save Newchurch Guinea Pigs: interim harassment injunction in animal rights campaign
key_facts: The Hall family bred guinea pigs for medical research at Darley Oaks Farm, Newchurch, and faced a sustained animal rights campaign from 1999.
Campaigners targeted employees, contractors, neighbours and local businesses with intimidation, criminal damage, grave desecration and arson.
Hodge J granted an interim injunction on 2 December 2004 restraining harassment while permitting limited Sunday demonstrations.
At the return date Owen J continued the injunction against additional defendants but refused a 200 sq km exclusion zone.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Return date hearing on an interim injunction under the Protection from Harassment Act 1997 in representative proceedings against animal rights protesters.
enrichment.outcome: Interim injunction continued against all defendants with terms on demonstration frequency, duration, location and numbers; exclusion zone application refused for the present; extended representative order for additional parishes refused.
enrichment.ratio: Harassment injunctions may restrain unlawful intimidation while balancing Article 10 and 11 rights under the Cream Holdings threshold; a wide exclusion zone is draconian and not necessary where a tailored injunction may suffice, though public order powers had not prevented the guerrilla campaign.
legal_issues: Whether interim injunction should bind additional named defendants
Appropriate limits on lawful protest under Articles 10 and 11
Whether a large exclusion zone was necessary and proportionate
Representative standing of a parish councillor for neighbouring communities
linked_authorities: Cream Holdings Ltd v Banerjee [2004] UKHL 44
Burris v Azadani [1995] 1 WLR 1373
University of Oxford v Animal Aid [2004] EWHC 2543 (QB)

confidence.notes: Four discrete issues and detailed campaign chronology are clearly resolved though trial merits remain untried.

notes: DRC asylum credibility appeal; Wilson J held adjudicator erred by separating expert medical evidence from credibility findings.

enrichment.short_title: Mibanga v SSHD: flawed credibility assessment in DRC Mai-Mai asylum appeal
key_facts: A Congolese appellant claimed lengthy RCD-Goma detention and torture after Mai-Mai association following his father-in-law's killing.
Professor Pottier and Dr Norman provided expert reports supporting the plausibility of his account and documenting extensive scarring including genital torture marks.
The adjudicator found core aspects wholly not credible before considering the medical evidence, which she said did not assist.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal upheld the adjudicator; the Court of Appeal remitted for redetermination.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on a point of law from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal dismissing an asylum and human rights appeal against refusal of asylum.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; adjudicator's determination and tribunal decision set aside; case remitted to a differently constituted adjudicator.
enrichment.ratio: A fact-finder must survey all relevant evidence before reaching credibility conclusions; expert medical and country evidence must be treated as an integral part of the credibility enquiry, not addressed only after adverse findings, and conclusory rejection of expert views requires reasoned explanation.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator erred by deferring consideration of medical evidence
Proper use of expert country and medical reports in credibility assessment
Internal relocation to Kinshasa and risk on return to the DRC
Article 8 family life with wife and children granted exceptional leave
index_terms: Medical Foundation for Care of Victims of Torture
linked_authorities: HE (DRC - Credibility and Psychiatric Reports) [2004] UKIAT 00321

confidence.notes: Procedural error analysis and remittal order are clearly reasoned across three judgments.

notes: CCRC reference on drug-supply manslaughter; Court of Appeal confirms joint administration under section 23 OAPA 1861 and dismisses appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Kennedy (No 2): manslaughter by joint administration of heroin for immediate injection
key_facts: Simon Kennedy prepared a syringe of heroin and handed it to Marco Bosque for immediate injection in a hostel room; Bosque injected himself and died.
Kennedy was convicted of manslaughter and supplying a Class A drug; an earlier appeal had been dismissed in 1998.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred the case because later decisions in Dias, Rogers and Finlay cast doubt on the reasoning.
The jury were directed that handing heroin for immediate injection could be a significant cause of death.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal following CCRC reference under section 9 of the Criminal Appeal Act 1995 on manslaughter by unlawful act after heroin self-injection.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction held safe where defendant and deceased were jointly engaged in administering heroin under section 23.
enrichment.ratio: Where a supplier prepares a syringe and hands it to the user for immediate injection as part of one combined administration, they may commit an unlawful act under section 23 and manslaughter if death results; self-injection alone is not a crime so encouragement without participation is insufficient, but joint administration avoids novus actus difficulties.
legal_issues: Whether supply of heroin for immediate self-injection supports manslaughter after Dalby
Distinction between principal under section 23 and accessory to non-existent self-manslaughter
Application of Dias, Rogers and Finlay to CCRC reference
Whether Empress causation principles apply to manslaughter
linked_authorities: R v Dalby (1982) 74 Cr App R 348
R v Dias [2002] 2 Cr App R 5
R v Rogers [2003] 1 WLR 1374
R v Finlay [2003] EWCA Crim 3868

confidence.notes: Extended review of post-Dalby authorities and affirmation of first appeal reasoning on joint responsibility.

notes: Leasehold enfranchisement stale claim; Court of Appeal held tenant at will after long lease obtained no Part IV secure tenancy protection.

enrichment.short_title: Banjo v Brent: no secure tenancy protection after long leasehold enfranchisement claim lapsed
key_facts: Mr Banjo held a long lease of a Brent dwelling house from the 1880s lease, served a section 5 enfranchisement notice in January 1980, but withdrew in March 1982 for lack of finance.
He remained in occupation paying no rent; Brent issued possession proceedings in 2002 after serving notice.
The county court dismissed his enfranchisement claim as time-barred but refused Brent's possession claim, holding he was a secure tenant.
The tenancy at will was determined by Brent's February 2002 notice before proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court order refusing a landlord's Part 20 possession claim after dismissing the tenant's enfranchisement claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; possession order granted; tenant at will after expiry of extended long lease did not acquire Part IV secure tenancy protection.
enrichment.ratio: Where a long tenancy from a local authority expires after a lapsed 1967 Act claim, the tenant holds over as tenant at will under general law; section 86 of the Housing Act 1985 does not convert a non-secure long tenancy into a secure periodic tenancy, and a determined tenancy at will affords no Part IV security.
legal_issues: When the long lease terminated after withdrawal of the enfranchisement claim
Whether a tenancy at will can be a secure tenancy under Part IV of the Housing Act 1985
Application of section 86 to long tenancies from local authorities
Effect of notice determining a tenancy at will before possession proceedings
linked_authorities: Harrison v Hammersmith and Fulham London Borough Council [1981] 1 WLR 650
Chamberlain v Farr [1943] 112 LJKB 206
Crane v Morris [1965] 1 WLR 1104

confidence.notes: Statutory scheme analysis and tenancy-at-will conclusion are comprehensively reasoned by Chadwick LJ.
